newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS SPOTLIGHT-KOURNIKOVA JOINS QUEUE FOR PLACE IN NEW ORDER. [CORRECTED 21:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: TENNIS SPOTLIGHT-KOURNIKOVA JOINS QUEUE FOR PLACE IN NEW ORDER. [CORRECTED 21:00 GMT]

text.p: The year 1997 may go down in the world annals as the year of the handover, not just in Hong Kong, but also in women's tennis, and on Wednesday Anna Kournikova underlined her bid for a place at the helm of the new order.

The 16-year-old Russian ruthlessly disposed of French Open champion Iva Majoli 7-6 6-4 in one hour and 19 minutes to become the second youngest women's singles semifinalist at Wimbledon after Jennifer Capriati, who at 15 years and three months, reached the same stage in 1991.

Ranked 42 in the world, she will move up at least 20 places in next week's rankings following her stunning victory -- her first semifinal appearance on the women's tour since turning professional in October 1995.
Majoli, the fourth seed, had no answer to the Russian's brute power and athleticism, and rarely left the baseline hoping her younger rival would slip and make an error.
The Florida-based Kournikova, who beat seventh seed Anke Huber and veteran Helena Sukova en route to the quarter-finals, rarely obliged and saved her most ferocious winners for the key points.

A mouth-watering semifinal between Wimbledon debutante Kournikova and another prodigy Martina Hingis will assure one or the other a place in the record books as the youngest Wimbledon finalist in the Open era beating the previous record of 18 years (corrects from 19 years) by Steffi Graf in 1987 (corrects from 1988).

Hingis, nine months older than Kournikova, has already assumed the mantle of successor to Steffi Graf's throne after becoming the youngest grand slam champion this century by winning the Australian Open in January and subsequently taking over at the top of the world rankings.
"She's a different player on grass...she's much better here," said top seeded Hingis of her rival. "Until now I always have beaten her pretty easily.
Kournikova, with her plaited long blond hair swinging like a pendulum each time she attacked the ball, on Wednesday joined the queue as a mover and shaker in the new order.

On centre court, the two East Europeans dropped their serve three times in the opening set, but Kournikova controlled the tie-break, passing Majoli with stinging forehands and whipping double-handed backhands.
The Croat bowed to the pressure and double-faulted at set point, handing her the tie-break 7-1.
They exchanged early breaks in the second set, but the inexperienced Kournikova again held her nerve at the pressure points holding her service to love to lead 5-4.
She then went on a full-scale attack against a wilting Majoli grabbing three match points and fired a scorching forehand winner down the line to clinch the match.
Majoli became the only player to beat Hingis this year when she defeated the Swiss in the French Open final last month.
"Her shots were hard and very deep...she was more aggressive than me and she was taking the chances and she was playing very risky," said Majoli.
"I gave her a chance to play, and especially on grass, the one who is attacking usually wins."
